title: Turning a few keywords into a sentence with two word predictors that meet in the middle
paper_title: Caption Generation from Keywords using Probabilistic Dual-LSTM Networks and Dynamic Programming
date_note: ICETSD '19 (copyright line 2019 GCELT; publisher PDF created 31 Mar 2019). Exact conference days not in the PDF and not certain from memory, so a plausible late-March day was chosen
venue: International Conference on Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Development (ICETSD)
authors: S Dubey, Swarnendu Ghosh, S Chowdhury, N Das, T Gonçalves, P Quaresma
summary: Given only a few keywords, such as the objects and places in a photo, how do you get a fluent sentence? We trained two language models, one reading forwards and one backwards, and joined their guesses.

body.p: Many systems know what is in a picture or a conversation, but only as a handful of keywords: "dog", "beach", "running". Turning those keywords into a natural sentence is harder than it looks, especially when there is no template or ready-made language model to lean on. We trained two word-prediction networks, one reading sentences forwards and one backwards, and built sentences from the places where their guesses meet.

Systems such as virtual assistants, chatbots and caption generators often pass information along as keywords. The final sentence still has to be fluent. Older approaches used grammar-like language models or statistical models of word sequences. We wanted something that learns from text alone and does not need a schema describing the sentence in advance.

We use a type of network called an LSTM (long short-term memory), which reads a sentence word by word and keeps a memory of what came before. Given the words so far, it gives a probability for each possible next word. We trained two of them on the same sentences. The forward LSTM learned the sentences as written. The reverse LSTM learned them back to front. This looks like the common bidirectional LSTM, but it is used differently: our two networks run separately at test time and are joined afterwards.

Take two keywords, W<sub>s</sub> and W<sub>e</sub>. We want a short phrase that starts with the first and ends with the second. The forward LSTM starts from W<sub>s</sub> and, at each step, keeps its K most probable next words. For each of those it again keeps K words, and so on, up to a depth L. That gives a tree of possible continuations. The reverse LSTM grows a similar tree backwards from W<sub>e</sub>.

figure.alt: Two branching trees of words: the forward tree grows to the right from the start keyword, and the reverse tree grows to the left from the end keyword, each with branching probabilities.
figure.caption: Each LSTM grows a tree of likely next words, one forward from the first keyword and one backward from the last.

body.p: A phrase is then found wherever a word in one tree matches a word in the other. To avoid chance matches, we also require one extra neighbouring word on each side to overlap. The phrase is scored by multiplying the probabilities of its words, and for the overlapping words we average the forward and reverse probabilities. A full sentence is made by chaining phrases for each neighbouring keyword pair and averaging their scores. We try every possible order of the keywords and rank the resulting sentences.

figure.alt: A diagram of a forward word chain and a reverse word chain overlapping in the middle, with the sentence score formula below.
figure.caption: Where the forward and reverse chains overlap, the two probabilities are averaged, and the overall sentence score is the product along the chain.

body.p: We trained on 404,207 sentences from the COCO caption data set, with two stacked LSTM layers of 650 units and 650-dimensional Word2Vec word vectors, over 23,000 distinct words. We tested on a different collection. We hand-annotated 500 randomly chosen images from the SBU data set with keywords for the objects, places, actions and attributes in them. We used a different training set on purpose, to show that the method is not tied to one corpus.

Three judges looked at the top five sentences for each keyword order and picked the best one. They scored four things out of 5. The first score asks how good the sentence is given the keywords. The second asks how well it describes the image. The third compares it with the image's real caption, and the fourth rates how well the real caption describes the image.

body.callout: Mean judge scores for the generated sentences were 4.90 for fit to the keywords and 4.89 for describing the image. The original captions in that test scored 2.72.

body.p: The third score, comparing our sentence with the actual caption, averaged 4.65 across the judges. The judges did not agree entirely: one gave 4.73 and 4.74 on the first two scores where the others gave close to 5. The paper puts the low score of the original captions down to "the whims of the human mind", which is an explanation it offers, not something it tested.

The evaluation is small and subjective. It covers 500 images, the keywords were chosen by hand by us, and the scores come from three judges rather than from an automatic metric. We did not compare against any other caption system, so the results say that the sentences are acceptable to people, not that they are better than other methods. The paper itself describes the results as "quite acceptable" in human terms.

Everything was in English, and the paper leaves other languages as future work. It also suggests trying the method on dialogue and question answering, where keywords from one component have to become a sentence for the user.
